topics.title: Vector algebra
topics.notes:
A vector has both size (magnitude) and direction; a scalar has size only. Velocity, force, momentum and acceleration are vectors; speed, mass, time and energy are scalars. In three dimensions a vector is written a = xi + yj + zk, where i, j and k are unit vectors along the x, y and z axes. Add or subtract vectors component by component: (3i + 6j) + (i − 2j) = 4i + 4j. A scalar multiple scales every component.

The magnitude (length) of a is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²). A common slip is to forget to take the square root, or to square a negative component wrongly: (−1)² = 1. When a question says "the magnitude is 7", write |a|² = 49 and solve; this often gives two values (for example (γ + 1)² = 9 gives γ = 2 or −4). Check each root against the wording: a magnitude can never be negative.

A unit vector in the direction of a is a divided by |a|, so its length is exactly 1. For a = 2i + 5j − k, |a| = √30 and the unit vector is (1/√30)(2i + 5j − k). The direction cosines (l, m, n) are the components divided by the length, so they are the components of the unit vector, and l² + m² + n² = 1 always. For r = 3i − 2j + 6k, |r| = 7 and (l, m, n) = (3/7, −2/7, 6/7).

The triangle law says AB + BC = AC, and BA = −AB. So AB + BC − DC − AD = AC − (AD + DC) = AC − AC = 0, the zero vector (not the number 1). The resultant of two vectors is their sum. To find unknown scalars in c = γa + βb, match the i, j and k components and solve the simultaneous equations.

KEY FORMULA: |a| = √(x² + y² + z²);  unit vector = a/|a|;  direction cosines = (x, y, z)/|a|;  AB + BC = AC
topics.keyFormula: |a| = √(x² + y² + z²);  unit vector = a/|a|;  direction cosines = (x, y, z)/|a|;  AB + BC = AC

topics.title: Dot and cross products
topics.notes:
There are two ways to multiply vectors, and they give different kinds of answer. The dot (scalar) product a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ gives a number. It also equals |a||b|cos θ, so it is zero when the vectors are perpendicular. For a = (2, 0, 3) and b = (5, −1, 1): a·b = 10 + 0 + 3 = 13.

The cross (vector) product a × b gives a vector perpendicular to both. With a = (a₁, a₂, a₃) and b = (b₁, b₂, b₃): a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁). Order matters: b × a = −(a × b). Also i × j = k, j × k = i and k × i = j. For p = (3, −4, 2) and q = (2, 5, −1): p × q = (4 − 10, 4 + 3, 15 + 8) = (−6, 7, 23). Work out each component in turn; sign slips in the middle component are the commonest error.

Watch the order of operations. In 2a·(b + 3c), first work out b + 3c (a vector), then take the dot product with 2a (giving a number). In (a·c)b, the bracket is a number, so the result is that number times the vector b, which is a vector. Always ask "will this step give a number or a vector?" before you compute it.

KEY FORMULA: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ (a number);  a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) (a vector)
topics.keyFormula: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ (a number);  a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) (a vector)

topics.title: Points, distance and straight lines
topics.notes:
For two points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): the distance is d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), the midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2) and the gradient is m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). If you know the midpoint and one end, double the midpoint and subtract the known end to find the other end: N = 2 × midpoint − M.

Two lines are parallel when their gradients are equal (m₁ = m₂) and perpendicular when m₁m₂ = −1. The line through (x₁, y₁) with gradient m is y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). A line parallel to ax + by + c = 0 keeps the same a and b, and only c changes: substitute the given point to find the new c. Always check by putting the point back into your final equation.

To find where two lines meet, solve their equations simultaneously, for example 3x + y = 7 and 4x + 2y = 10 meet at (2, 1). To find the line from a given point to that intersection, find the gradient between the two points and use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Distance questions often give an unknown coordinate: set the distance formula equal to the given value, square both sides, and solve. For (x − 2)² + 16 = 41 you get x − 2 = ±5, so there are two answers, x = 7 and x = −3. Expanding (1 − β)² + (α − 1)² and using α + β = 2 is a good way to find α² + β² without solving for α and β.

KEY FORMULA: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²);  m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁);  perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1;  y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
topics.keyFormula: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²);  m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁);  perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1;  y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)

topics.title: Circles and conics
topics.notes:
A circle with centre (h, k) and radius r has equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Expanding gives the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, which has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). To go from the general form to the centre and radius, complete the square: x² + y² + 4x − 6y + 12 = 0 becomes (x + 2)² + (y − 3)² = 1, so the centre is (−2, 3) and r = 1.

The length of the tangent from an outside point (x₁, y₁) to the circle is √(x₁² + y₁² + 2gx₁ + 2fy₁ + c): just substitute the point into the left side of the circle equation and take the square root. For (7, 5) and x² + y² − 4x − 6y + 9 = 0 the value is √25 = 5. If the number under the root is negative, the point is inside the circle.

The standard forms centred at the origin are: parabola opening right y² = 4ax; ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1; hyperbola with horizontal transverse axis x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. For the hyperbola the foci are (±ae, 0), the directrices are x = ±a/e and b² = a²(e² − 1). Given foci (±9, 0) and directrices x = ±4, ae = 9 and a/e = 4, so a² = 36, e = 3/2 and b² = 45.

A tangent "at a point" only makes sense if the point lies on the curve: check by substituting its coordinates first. For y² = 4ax the tangent at (x₁, y₁) is yy₁ = 2a(x + x₁).

KEY FORMULA: Circle: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²;  parabola y² = 4ax;  ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1;  hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, b² = a²(e² − 1)
topics.keyFormula: Circle: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²;  parabola y² = 4ax;  ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1;  hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, b² = a²(e² − 1)

topics.title: Kinematics: position, velocity and acceleration
topics.notes:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Velocity is the rate of change of position, v = ds/dt (or dr/dt for a vector), and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt = d²r/dt². To go the other way, integrate: v = ∫a dt and s = ∫v dt. The constants of integration come from the starting conditions, such as s = 0 at t = 0.

For motion in a plane or in space, treat each coordinate separately. For r = (3t², 8t, 3t³): velocity is (6t, 8, 9t²) and acceleration is (6, 0, 18t). Differentiate first and substitute the time afterwards, never the other way round. At t = 2 this gives r = (12, 16, 24), v = (12, 8, 36) and a = (6, 0, 36).

The magnitude of a vector in motion questions uses the usual formula: for a = (6, 0, 24) the magnitude is √(36 + 576) = √612. Do not confuse √612 with 612. Mass is not needed for position, velocity or acceleration; it only matters once forces, energy or momentum are involved.

Be careful with the question wording: "position", "velocity" and "acceleration" each need a different number of derivatives. For s = 5t³ + 3t², the acceleration at t = 3 is 30t + 6 = 96. If the velocity is given as a function of time, integrate once to get the position, and once more would be needed only if the position is already given as a function of time and you want something else.

For exponential and trigonometric paths, remember d/dt e⁻ᵗ = −e⁻ᵗ, d/dt cos 5t = −5 sin 5t and d/dt sin 5t = 5 cos 5t. The factor 5 comes out each time you differentiate, so the second derivative has a factor of 25.

KEY FORMULA: v = dr/dt;  a = dv/dt = d²r/dt²;  s = ∫v dt;  v = ∫a dt  (constants from the starting conditions)
topics.keyFormula: v = dr/dt;  a = dv/dt = d²r/dt²;  s = ∫v dt;  v = ∫a dt  (constants from the starting conditions)

topics.title: Force and equations of motion
topics.notes:
Newton's second law says F = ma = d(mv)/dt: force is the rate of change of momentum. Impulse is force × time and equals the change in momentum, so it is not the same thing as force. For a constant force acting over a displacement, work = F × d, so F = work ÷ displacement is also true. In vector problems, find the acceleration first and multiply every component by the mass.

When the force varies with time, use a = F/m and integrate. For a 5 kg particle starting at rest under F = (7t + t²) N: a = (7t + t²)/5, v = 7t²/10 + t³/15, and s = 7t³/30 + t⁴/60. After 3 s, v = 8.1 m/s and s = 7.65 m. Each integration needs its own starting condition (v = 0 and s = 0 at t = 0).

To write an equation of motion with air resistance, first choose which direction is positive, then add up the forces. Shot upward (upward positive): gravity and resistance both act downward, so v′ = −g − kv. Falling (downward positive): gravity helps and resistance opposes, so v′ = g − kv. If the resistance is proportional to v², replace kv with kv². The mass M divides out of every term when the resistance is Mkv.

Common traps: reporting the acceleration when the question asks for the force (or the reverse); forgetting to multiply by the mass; and picking an option such as v′ = Mg − kv whose terms do not all have the same units.

KEY FORMULA: F = ma;  v = ∫(F/m) dt;  upward: v′ = −g − kv;  falling: v′ = g − kv
topics.keyFormula: F = ma;  v = ∫(F/m) dt;  upward: v′ = −g − kv;  falling: v′ = g − kv

topics.title: Work, energy and power
topics.notes:
Work is force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of the force, W = Fd, measured in joules. Lifting a mass m through a height h against gravity needs W = mgh. Only the vertical rise counts: a particle that reaches (x, y) = (2, 3) m does work against gravity of 25 × 9.8 × 3 = 735 J, and the 2 m sideways adds nothing.

Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, measured in watts. Dividing the 735 J above by 3 s gives 245 W. When the force and velocity are vectors, the instantaneous power is the dot product P = F·v. For a 4 kg particle at t = 4 with F = (2112, 384) N and v = (672, 197) m/s, P = 2112 × 672 + 384 × 197 ≈ 1.49 × 10⁶ W.

Kinetic energy is KE = ½mv², where v² is the square of the speed. For a velocity (5, 3) m/s, v² = 25 + 9 = 34, so a 10 kg particle has KE = ½ × 10 × 34 = 170 J. Work done by the total force on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy.

When the force changes with time, W = F·d with the final force is not correct, because the force at the end is not the force all along the path. Use the work-energy idea (change in kinetic energy) or integrate F·v over time.

KEY FORMULA: W = Fd (lifting: W = mgh);  P = W/t = F·v;  KE = ½mv²
topics.keyFormula: W = Fd (lifting: W = mgh);  P = W/t = F·v;  KE = ½mv²
